html:
Chandragupta II was emperor of the Gupta Empire from about 375 or 380 to about 415, when it reached its greatest size and wealth. He took the title Vikramaditya, "sun of valour". His birth date is unknown.

He was a son of Samudragupta. His greatest conquest was the defeat of the Western Satraps, the last Saka rulers of western India, around 400. That gave the Guptas Gujarat, Malwa and the rich ports of the Arabian Sea coast. To secure the south he married his daughter Prabhavatigupta to the king of the Vakatakas; after her husband died she ruled that kingdom as regent, keeping it close to her father's.

His reign is remembered as a high point of classical Indian culture:

  • The Chinese monk Faxian, who travelled in India in his time, found the land peaceful and well governed, with light punishments.
  • The iron pillar of Delhi names a king Chandra, usually taken to be him.
  • He issued fine gold coins, some showing him killing a lion.
  • Legend places the poet Kalidasa among the "nine gems" of his court, though this is not certain.

The figure of King Vikramaditya in later Indian stories owes much to his memory. His son Kumaragupta I followed him.
